title: Causes and Conduct of World War II
subject: AP World History
objectives: Analyze the causes of World War II, including fascist/militarist aggression, the failure of appeasement, and the unresolved tensions of WWI
Describe the global scope and major theaters of World War II in Europe, the Pacific, Africa, and Asia
Explain how World War II was a 'total war' that mobilized entire societies and deliberately targeted civilians
Analyze the major consequences of World War II, including the death toll, the use of atomic weapons, and the new global order

sections.heading: A Piece of Paper Promising Peace
sections.content:
On September 30, 1938, the British Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain stepped off an airplane in London, waved a piece of paper to the cheering crowd, and declared that he had secured 'peace for our time.' He had just returned from a conference in Munich where Britain and France agreed to let Adolf Hitler annex a large part of Czechoslovakia, in exchange for his promise to make no further demands. Many people genuinely believed a second world war had been avoided. Less than a year later, Hitler invaded Poland, and the world was at war again. Chamberlain's piece of paper has become one of history's most famous symbols of a failed strategy — APPEASEMENT — and of the dangerous illusion that an aggressor's appetite can be satisfied by giving in to it.

World War II would become the deadliest conflict in human history, killing an estimated 60 to 80 million people — more than three times the toll of World War I. It was fought on a truly global scale, from the steppes of Russia to the jungles of Burma to the islands of the Pacific to the deserts of North Africa. It saw the deliberate mass killing of civilians become a central feature of war, culminating in the Holocaust and the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki. And it ended with two new superpowers, the United States and the Soviet Union, standing astride a ruined world — setting the stage for the Cold War that dominates Unit 8.

This lesson examines both why World War II happened and how it was fought. The causes connect directly back to the previous lesson: the unresolved tensions of WWI and the totalitarian regimes born of the Depression. The conduct of the war reveals the terrifying maturity of 'total war,' now waged with even greater technological power and even fewer limits on the killing of civilians.

sections.heading: The Causes: Aggression and Appeasement
sections.content:
World War II had both long-term and immediate causes, and a strong answer connects them. The LONG-TERM causes are the unresolved tensions you studied in the last lesson: the bitter, vengeful legacy of the Treaty of Versailles, the global economic devastation of the Great Depression, and the rise of aggressive, expansionist totalitarian regimes — Nazi Germany, fascist Italy, and militarist Japan — that saw conquest as the path to national greatness and to solving their economic problems.

The more IMMEDIATE causes were the chain of aggressions by these powers in the 1930s and the failure of the democracies to stop them. JAPAN invaded Manchuria in 1931 and launched a full-scale, brutal war against China in 1937. ITALY invaded Ethiopia in 1935 (avenging its earlier defeat at Adwa). And Nazi GERMANY rearmed in violation of Versailles, remilitarized the Rhineland, annexed Austria, and then demanded Czechoslovakia. In each case the League of Nations and the major democracies failed to respond effectively. Britain and France pursued APPEASEMENT — giving in to Hitler's demands in the hope of avoiding war — most infamously at the Munich Conference of 1938. Appeasement failed catastrophically because it only convinced Hitler that the democracies were weak and would not fight. The immediate spark came on September 1, 1939, when Germany — having secured the Nazi-Soviet Pact (a cynical non-aggression deal with Stalin to divide Eastern Europe) — invaded POLAND, and Britain and France finally declared war.

Notice the causation structure, which mirrors WWI: deep underlying causes (Versailles, the Depression, totalitarian ideology) made aggression likely, a chain of specific aggressions escalated the danger, the failure of appeasement removed the brakes, and the invasion of Poland was the immediate trigger. This is the same layered, long-term-versus-immediate analysis the whole unit has been training — now applied to the second great war.

sections.question: Why did the policy of appeasement, seen most clearly at the 1938 Munich Conference, fail to prevent World War II?
options: It provoked Hitler into making peace
By giving in to Hitler's demands (such as a large part of Czechoslovakia), it convinced him the democracies were weak and would not fight, encouraging further aggression rather than satisfying him
It successfully stopped all German expansion
It had no effect on Hitler's decisions at all
sections.explanation: Appeasement — conceding to Hitler's demands to avoid war — failed because it signaled weakness. Rather than satisfying Hitler, the Munich concessions emboldened him; within a year he seized the rest of Czechoslovakia and invaded Poland. Appeasement is a classic example of how trying to avoid conflict by yielding to an aggressor can invite it.

sections.heading: A Global War on Many Fronts
sections.content:
World War II was even more genuinely global than the first, fought across multiple major theaters that the AP exam expects you to recognize. In EUROPE, Germany unleashed BLITZKRIEG ('lightning war') — fast, coordinated assaults by tanks, aircraft, and infantry — to conquer Poland, then France and much of Western Europe by 1940, leaving Britain to fight on alone through the aerial Battle of Britain. In 1941 Hitler made his fateful decision to invade the SOVIET UNION (breaking the Nazi-Soviet Pact), opening a colossal and savage Eastern Front where the bulk of the war's fighting and dying took place; the Soviet victory at STALINGRAD (1942–43) became the turning point in Europe. North Africa and Italy saw hard fighting too, and the Western Allies opened a second front with the D-DAY landings in Normandy in June 1944, squeezing Germany between advancing American-British and Soviet armies until it surrendered in May 1945.

In the PACIFIC and ASIA, Japan sought to build a vast empire (the 'Greater East Asia Co-Prosperity Sphere'), conquering much of Southeast Asia and the Pacific after its surprise attack on the U.S. naval base at PEARL HARBOR in December 1941 brought the United States fully into the war. The U.S. fought back across the Pacific in a brutal 'island-hopping' campaign, with the turning point at the Battle of MIDWAY (1942). The war in China, where Japan had been fighting since 1937, was vast and devastating. And the conflict reached Africa, the Middle East, and the world's oceans.

As in WWI, the combatants drew on their global EMPIRES — millions of colonial troops and laborers from India, Africa, and elsewhere fought and worked for the Allied (and Axis) war efforts, again raising expectations of post-war self-rule. The two alliances were the AXIS (Germany, Italy, Japan) and the ALLIES (led by Britain, the Soviet Union, the United States, and China). The sheer geographic spread — Europe, the USSR, the Pacific, China, Southeast Asia, North Africa, the Atlantic — is why this was the most global war in history.

sections.heading: Major Theaters and Turning Points of World War II
rows: Blitzkrieg conquers France (1940); Battle of Britain; D-Day (1944)
German invasion of USSR (1941); most of the war's casualties
Japan's war on China from 1937; mass atrocities
Prolonged resistance ties down Japanese forces
Desert campaigns; Battle of the Atlantic (U-boats)

sections.content: World War II grew from the unresolved tensions of WWI and the rise of aggressive totalitarian regimes; enabled by failed appeasement, it became the deadliest, most global 'total war' in history, deliberately targeting civilians and ending with atomic weapons and two new superpowers.
sections.heading: Core Takeaway

sections.question: Which event brought the United States fully into World War II?
options: The German invasion of Poland in 1939
The Japanese surprise attack on the U.S. naval base at Pearl Harbor in December 1941
sections.explanation: Japan's surprise attack on Pearl Harbor on December 7, 1941, brought the United States fully into the war (against Japan, and then Germany, which declared war on the U.S.). The invasion of Poland began the war in Europe; Munich was an act of appeasement; Stalingrad was a turning point on the Eastern Front.

sections.heading: Total War Without Limits: Targeting Civilians
sections.content:
World War II carried the concept of TOTAL WAR (from the last lesson) to an even more extreme and terrible degree, and one feature above all defines it: the deliberate, mass targeting of CIVILIANS became central to how the war was fought. In WWI most of the dead were soldiers; in WWII, the majority of the roughly 60–80 million dead were civilians. This is one of the most important things to understand about the war's conduct.

Civilians were targeted in several ways. STRATEGIC BOMBING deliberately attacked enemy cities to destroy industry and break civilian morale — the German bombing of British cities (the Blitz), and far more destructively, the Allied firebombing of cities like Hamburg, Dresden, and Tokyo, which killed tens of thousands of civilians in single nights. OCCUPATION regimes, especially Nazi Germany's in Eastern Europe and Japan's in China and Southeast Asia, were murderously brutal, marked by massacres, forced labor, starvation, and systematic atrocities such as the Rape of Nanjing. And the most extreme case was the HOLOCAUST, the Nazi regime's deliberate, industrialized genocide of six million Jews, along with millions of Roma, disabled people, Soviet prisoners, political prisoners, and others — a state-organized program of mass murder that you will examine as a case study in the unit's final lesson.

The war reached its terrible climax with a new weapon. To force Japan's surrender and avoid a costly invasion, the United States dropped ATOMIC BOMBS on the cities of HIROSHIMA and NAGASAKI in August 1945, killing well over a hundred thousand people, mostly civilians, in two blinding flashes. Japan surrendered days later. The atomic bomb was the ultimate expression of industrialized total war — the power to annihilate an entire city in an instant — and its shadow would hang over the entire Cold War era you are about to study. The deliberate targeting of civilians, by all sides and culminating in genocide and nuclear weapons, is the defining moral horror of how WWII was conducted.

sections.heading: Why the Eastern Front Changes the Whole Story
sections.content:
Many students picture WWII through the Western lens — D-Day, the Blitz, Pearl Harbor — and miss where the war was actually decided. Let's correct that with the evidence. Of the roughly 60 to 80 million who died in WWII, the Soviet Union alone lost an estimated 27 million people, the overwhelming majority of them on the Eastern Front against Germany. For comparison, the United States lost about 400,000 and Britain about 450,000. The scale is not close.

Now reason about what those numbers mean. From 1941, the bulk of the German army was committed against the USSR, not the West, and it was there — at Stalingrad, Kursk, and across a thousand miles of brutal fighting — that Germany's military was ground down before the Western Allies ever landed at Normandy in 1944. This is a case where DEMOGRAPHIC evidence (casualty figures) drives a CAUSAL argument: a fair account of why the Allies won must center the Eastern Front, where Nazi Germany was primarily defeated. It is also where the war was most genocidal, the setting for the Holocaust's death camps and the murder of millions of Soviet civilians and POWs.

The analytical lesson is about avoiding a Eurocentric or Americentric distortion the AP exam specifically guards against. A strong essay on WWII does not treat it as a Western story with a Pacific sideshow; it recognizes a genuinely multi-front, multi-regional war in which the Eastern Front was decisive and the war in China had raged since 1937. When you marshal evidence for any 'why did X win or happen' argument, ask where the weight of the evidence actually lies — here, the casualty numbers point unmistakably east.

steps.title: Anchor the underlying (long-term) causes
steps.content: Begin with the deep conditions: the Treaty of Versailles' bitter legacy, the Great Depression, and the rise of expansionist totalitarian regimes. These explain why aggression became likely. For WWII, the unresolved tensions of WWI are the bedrock long-term cause.

steps.title: Add the chain of immediate causes
steps.content: Layer the specific triggering events: Axis aggressions (Japan in Manchuria/China, Italy in Ethiopia, German rearmament and expansion), the failure of appeasement at Munich, the Nazi-Soviet Pact, and the invasion of Poland in 1939. These explain the timing and the final outbreak.

steps.title: Explain how the causes interact
steps.content: Show the linkage: Versailles resentment + Depression desperation enabled Hitler's rise; Hitler's aggression met weak appeasement, which emboldened further aggression until Poland forced war. Demonstrating interaction — not a flat list — is what separates a top causation response.

steps.title: Take a defensible, prioritized position
steps.content: Argue a thesis about which causes mattered most — e.g., 'While long-term resentment of Versailles created the conditions, it was the failure to confront Axis aggression in the 1930s that made a second world war unavoidable.' A clear, arguable, prioritized thesis earns the highest causation score.

sections.heading: Common WWII Errors to Avoid
sections.content: Watch for these. (1) Do NOT reduce WWII's causes to 'Hitler was evil' — the exam wants the LAYERED causes: Versailles, the Depression, totalitarian expansionism, AND the failure of appeasement. (2) Do NOT forget the EASTERN FRONT, where the majority of the war's fighting and dying occurred; an account focused only on the Western democracies badly distorts the war (the USSR suffered ~27 million dead). (3) Do NOT treat WWII as beginning in 1939 everywhere — in Asia it began with Japan's invasion of China in 1937 (some date it to Manchuria in 1931). (4) Keep the alliances straight: AXIS = Germany, Italy, Japan; ALLIES = Britain, USSR, U.S., China. (5) Do NOT confuse the Holocaust (genocide of Jews and others) with the general civilian death toll — it was a specific, deliberate, industrialized program of extermination.

sections.heading: Compare WWI and WWII for Continuity and Change
sections.content: A favorite exam move is to compare the two world wars (a CCOT or comparison prompt). CONTINUITIES: both were global, total wars that mobilized whole societies and colonial empires, driven by nationalism and industrial technology, and both reshaped the global balance of power. CHANGES: WWII was far deadlier; civilians (not soldiers) were the majority of the dead; it featured deliberate genocide (the Holocaust), strategic bombing of cities, blitzkrieg mobility (vs. WWI's trench stalemate), and ended with atomic weapons and the rise of two superpowers rather than a multipolar Europe. Having three crisp continuities and three crisp changes ready lets you handle any WWI-to-WWII comparison or CCOT prompt with specific evidence.

sections.heading: Causes and Conduct of WWII Essentials
sections.content: CAUSES: LONG-TERM = Versailles resentment + GREAT DEPRESSION + totalitarian expansionism (Nazi Germany, fascist Italy, militarist Japan). IMMEDIATE = Axis aggressions (JAPAN: Manchuria 1931, China 1937; ITALY: Ethiopia 1935; GERMANY: rearming, Rhineland, Austria, Czechoslovakia) + failed APPEASEMENT (MUNICH 1938) + NAZI-SOVIET PACT → invasion of POLAND, Sept 1, 1939. THEATERS: EUROPE (BLITZKRIEG, fall of France 1940, Battle of Britain; D-DAY 1944); EASTERN FRONT (invasion of USSR 1941; STALINGRAD turning point; USSR ~27M dead); PACIFIC (PEARL HARBOR Dec 1941 brings in the U.S.; MIDWAY 1942; island-hopping); CHINA (from 1937). ALLIANCES: AXIS (Germany, Italy, Japan) vs. ALLIES (Britain, USSR, U.S., China). TOTAL WAR + CIVILIANS: most of the ~60–80M dead were civilians — STRATEGIC BOMBING (Blitz, Dresden, Tokyo), brutal OCCUPATION (Rape of Nanjing), the HOLOCAUST (6M Jews + millions of others), and ATOMIC BOMBS on HIROSHIMA & NAGASAKI (Aug 1945). RESULT: two superpowers (U.S. & USSR) → Cold War.

sections.heading: The War That Made the Modern World Order
sections.content:
World War II is the event from which the world you actually live in most directly descends, and its consequences set the agenda for the entire rest of the course. Consider the new global order it created. The old European great powers — Britain, France, Germany — were exhausted, bankrupted, or destroyed. In their place stood two SUPERPOWERS of a new kind: the United States, which emerged with its homeland untouched and its economy supercharged, and the Soviet Union, which had borne the heaviest fighting and now controlled Eastern Europe. The rivalry between these two, and between their competing ideologies of capitalist democracy and communism, would structure global politics for the next forty-five years as the COLD WAR — the entire subject of Unit 8.

The war also accelerated the end of the European empires that had dominated the previous units. The colonial powers were weakened and discredited; millions of colonial subjects had again fought in a war fought, supposedly, for freedom and against tyranny; and Japan's early conquests had shattered the myth of European invincibility in Asia. Within two decades of 1945, most of the world's colonies would be independent nations — the great wave of DECOLONIZATION you will study in Unit 8. The war also produced new institutions designed to prevent its recurrence: the UNITED NATIONS, replacing the failed League; new economic institutions; and, in response to the Holocaust, a new international language of human rights and the very concept of 'genocide.'

For the exam, this lesson ties the whole unit together and points forward to the next. It completes the unit's central CAUSATION arc — showing how WWI's unresolved tensions (Unit 7's earlier lessons) caused the interwar crisis, which caused WWII — and it sets up the comparison and CCOT links between the two wars. Most importantly, it delivers you to the doorstep of the postwar world: superpowers, the Cold War, decolonization, human rights, and the nuclear age. The next lesson, the unit's synthesis, will zoom in on the war's most extreme dimension — mass atrocity and genocide — to sharpen the causation reasoning you have been building and to confront the deepest questions this terrible century poses.
